events.text:
Last year, Trump tried reaching Kim Jong Un through established phone lines and communications channels. Nobody called back.
Trump next wrote a letter. White House officials hatched a plan for a group to wait outside the Manhattan office of North Korea’s permanent mission to the United Nations. When a North Korean diplomat walked past, the group swooped in and thrust the letter into his hands.
At a UN meeting, the diplomat later tossed the unopened letter in front of a U.S. representative.
Trump also sought a meeting with Kim during his latest Asia trip, but the North Korean leader reportedly set conditions Washington could not accept.
Since their last meeting in 2019, North Korea’s nuclear arsenal has grown from an estimated 20–30 warheads to around 60, while Pyongyang has developed intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of reaching the U.S.
Kim is now pushing for Washington to recognize North Korea as a nuclear power.
Source: WSJ

New satellite imagery reveals the extensive damage caused by an Iranian ballistic [missile strike on an Aero Sol facility in Petah Tikva](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/67675), near Tel Aviv, in April.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇺🇸💣 US military still short on weapons — and Pentagon has no master plan to fix it
The Pentagon is still struggling with persistent munitions shortages — yet has no department-wide plan linking weapons production and funding to what the US military actually needs, the Government Accountability Office reported.
The 2026 war against Iran has only increased pressure on already strained US stockpiles and the defense industrial base.
GAO’s findings paint a chaotic picture:
🌏 No master plan: DOD has no overarching strategy with long-term goals, implementation plans or metrics to measure whether shortages are actually being fixed.
🌏 Reactive production: the Army ramped up 155mm artillery shell production after shortages worsened through US support for allies — but the increase was not based on the Pentagon’s total munitions requirement.
🌏 $25 billion, still no roadmap: Congress appropriated at least $25bn in 2025 for munitions, while GAO warns the Pentagon risks both continuing shortages and spending on weapons beyond actual requirements.
🌏 Nobody fully in charge: no single Pentagon office has department-wide authority over the problem. The Munitions Acceleration Council, created in July 2025 to boost missile production, still had no formally signed charter in November 2026.
🌏 Even the inventory data is shaky: DOD’s Munitions Readiness Initiative draws from 37 data sources, but inventories are not consistently reconciled and the system has no documented data-management plan or data dictionary.
🌏 Aging industrial base: many Army ammunition facilities still rely on buildings, equipment and production processes dating back to the World War II era.
At the same time, GAO withheld classified details on persistent shortages and how they have affected US war plans.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

🇮🇱🇸🇾 IDF ramps up incursions into Syria, scouts vital water basin
Israel launched fresh ground operations in the Quneitra countryside in southern Syria on Saturday, making incursions into two local villages.
Sources told Al Bawaba News a young man was shot in the village of Bariqa, one of the targeted villages. No further details were provided about his condition or the circumstances leading to his shooting.
Separately, the IDF set up [a checkpoint](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78103) on a road between two towns in Quneitra’s north near the Golan Heights’ UN peacekeeping zone.
Intensive Israeli reconnaissance flights were also reported over the Yarmouk Basin in the western Daraa countryside. The area contains important water resources, dams, and fertile farmland. Yarmouk Basin water talks between Syria and neighboring Jordan took up special urgency this year after Israel refused to renew a landmark 2021 water-sharing agreement it had with[ Amman](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71785).
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights has counted 97 Israeli incursions into Syria from November 1-20, including raids, arrests, gunfire, shelling, movement restrictions, and land-clearing/excavation operations.
[The Syrian government ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73108)has paid lip-service to condemning Israel’s activities, but seems more focused on cracking down on [rebellious minorities](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75682) and sending military advisors to Saudi Arabia than securing its own borders.
